nameStory: Simocephalus serrulatus gets its scientific name from Greek words meaning 'flat-headed' and Latin 'serrulatus' meaning 'finely toothed like a saw.' This tiny water flea earned these names from its distinctively flattened head shape and the saw-like serrations along parts of its shell.
description: Simocephalus serrulatus is a microscopic water flea, one of the many tiny crustaceans that drift through freshwater ponds and lakes. These translucent creatures are about the size of a pinhead, measuring roughly 1-2 millimeters long. Through a magnifying glass or microscope, you can see their clear, helmet-like shell and watch their feathery swimming appendages beat rapidly like tiny oars. They're part of the zooplankton community - the drifting animal life that forms a crucial link in freshwater food webs.

idTips.label: Flattened Head Shape
idTips.description: The head region appears notably flattened from side to side, giving it a distinctive profile that's less rounded than other water fleas

idTips.label: Shell Serrations
idTips.description: Fine, tooth-like projections along the posterior edge of the transparent shell create a subtle saw-toothed appearance under magnification

idTips.label: Swimming Motion
idTips.description: Moves through water with characteristic jerky, hopping motions rather than smooth gliding, propelled by rapid beats of branched antennae

idTips.label: Body Size
idTips.description: Measures about 1-2 millimeters in length, roughly the size of a small pinhead and visible to the naked eye as a tiny moving speck

idTips.label: Transparency
idTips.description: Body appears glassy and nearly colorless, though may show faint yellowish or greenish tints depending on what they've been eating

habitat: Found in shallow, weedy areas of ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England's lowland regions. They prefer waters rich in organic matter and aquatic vegetation, often clustering near submerged plants or along muddy shorelines where algae and bacteria are abundant.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin building as waters warm, often appearing in temporary pools and newly ice-free pond edges where they reproduce rapidly.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm months when they're most active and easiest to spot in pond samples.
seasonality.fall: Numbers may decline but hardy individuals persist, often producing overwintering eggs as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Largely absent from the water column, surviving as dormant eggs in pond sediments until spring thaw.

funFact: *Note: Information about this rare species is limited due to only one recorded observation in New England - this description is based on general knowledge of the genus and may not be entirely accurate for this specific species.*
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other Simocephalus species and common water fleas like Daphnia, but the flattened head shape and serrated shell edges help distinguish it under magnification.
contextualKnowledge: This species appears to be extremely rare in New England with only a single recorded observation, so any sighting would be scientifically significant and worth documenting with photos if possible.
compareHints: Compared to its relative Simocephalus exspinosus, S. serrulatus typically has more pronounced shell serrations and a more distinctly flattened head profile. The serrated edges are the key distinguishing feature, as exspinosus tends to have smoother shell margins.
